* #### **Introduction** {#introduction}

  👋Welcome to the TeamAssign technical development team\! This document will walk you through the initial setups to get you started and provide some basic info you need to know. First, you need access to TeamAssign’s GitHub repository (where all the source code of the TeamAssign system is located) and the developer’s virtual machine (this is where you will do your development work) before proceeding to the sections below. If you don’t have access to them, please contact your supervisor 😊.  
    
  ⚠️Please note that the information in this document is subject to change and needs to be updated periodically due to the constant software dependency releases (especially the sections about Amazon Web Services and Canvas Integration).  


* #### **Public Crypto Key Setup 🔑** {#public-crypto-key-setup-🔑}

- A public crypto key is used to gain access to TeamAssign’s GitHub repository and remote access to the AWS instances used for development.   
- [This link](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/connecting-to-github-with-ssh/generating-a-new-ssh-key-and-adding-it-to-the-ssh-agent) contains detailed instructions on how to set up an SSH key and add it to the ssh-agent.  
- Next, add it to your GitHub account. Instructions are in [this link](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/connecting-to-github-with-ssh/adding-a-new-ssh-key-to-your-github-account).    
- Now, save the public key fingerprint of your SSH key; it will be used to grant you access to everything you need. Contact admin for more details.  
    
  ![][image1]  
    
  The result should look something like this. The covered part is where the public key fingerprint of your SSH key is.

* #### **Logging into the developer’s virtual machine ⚙️**  {#logging-into-the-developer’s-virtual-machine-⚙️}

- Type the following command into your terminal:   
    
  ssh \-A \<[yourName\>@\<devNum\>.teamassign.org](mailto:[REDACTED])  
    
  (Substitute devNum with dev01, dev02, or dev03 depending on which virtual instance you are trying to log into). The “\-A” part is used to forward your GitHub credentials to your virtual machine so you can commit code and submit pull requests; it can be placed after \<[yourName\>@\<devNum\>.teamassign.org](mailto:[REDACTED]) as well. Please contact the admin for more details.  
    
- If the above command doesn’t work, you might need to do:  
    
  ssh \-A \-i path-to-file \<[yourName\>@\<devNum\>.teamassign.org](mailto:[REDACTED])  
    
  Substitute devNum with dev01, dev02, dev03, etc., depending on which virtual instance you are trying to log into. Substitute path-to-file with the path of the file in which you store your SSH key on your local machine. The process of finding the file path may be different depending on the operating system of your local machine. Example: ssh \-i \~/.ssh/id\_ed25519/ [user@dev01.teamassign.org](mailto:[REDACTED])  
    
- If you need root access, first log into your developer instance, then run sudo \-i or sudo \-E su and enter your password to log in as root. Run exit when you need to exit root. Also, remember to change your root password after the initial setup. 

- In the dev machine, run cd /var/www/src to go to the location of the source code.  
    
- When working on code, it is advised to open three terminal windows and SSH each of them into the TeamAssign developer’s virtual machine. Connect one to the database, one to show error logs, and one to work on the actual code. Personally, I use vi/vim on the dev machine for development, but you are welcome to use any IDE you prefer.   
    
- The files are read-only so you need to run sudo vi \<filename\> to edit them. Type “:set number” inside Vim to see the line numbers before going into insert mode (To display line numbers by default, follow the instructions [here](https://www.cyberciti.biz/faq/vim-show-line-numbers-by-default-on-linux/).


- Type :w to save the changes you made, :q to quit the Vim interface without saving, and :wq to save the changes and quit the Vim interface.   
    
- For security reasons, errors will not be displayed in your browser so you will need to run make tail\_logs to see error messages. More information about make commands can be found in the Makefile.  
    
- When printing debugging messages or specific variables, Data::Dumper and warn are highly recommended. Data::Dumper is used when you need to see the details of a variable with references, like an array or a hash. Warn is used to print plain text messages. Example usages:


| warn "error message";use Data::Dumper; warn Dumper %hash;use Data::Dumper; warn Dumper $array; |
| :---- |


  The output will be visible when you run make tail\_logs. A lot of things are printed out in the logs (not just your debug output), so it is recommended to maybe add something in your debug messages to make it stand out more. For example: warn “……………………………start of debugging section”; Doing this will give you a clear mark of where the debugging is happening since the line number will also be printed out. It is also recommended to press the “enter” key a few times before a new debugging session so you can separate previous debug messages and new debug messages. 

		

- In most cases, you will only need to worry about the directories “teamassign” and “teamassign-lib” in the TeamAssign GitHub; that’s where most of the source code is. The part related to Canvas-LMS integration is under teamassign-lib/lib/LMS.   
    
- If you make changes in teamassign-lib, you need to restart the server to see the changes. To do this, go to the src directory in your dev machine and run make restart\_httpd.

* #### **SSH Sessions to Your Dev Machine Within VS Code**  {#ssh-sessions-to-your-dev-machine-within-vs-code}

  If you are more comfortable using VS Code for coding work compared to Vim, you can also do that. To add a virtual machine to VS Code, follow the steps below: 

1. Open your VS Code window and type “\> ssh” into the command palette at the top (Pressing command \+ p will make the command palette appear if you are using a MacBook). Choose “Remote-SSH: Add New SSH Host” from the drop-down menu.

   ![][image2]

2. Enter your SSH command ssh \-A \<[yourName\>@\<devNum\>.teamassign.org](mailto:[REDACTED]) and press “Enter”. 

   ![][image3]

3. Choose your SSH configuration file from the drop-down menu.   
4. A small pop-up will appear near the bottom of the window. Click on “Connect”. 

   ![][image4]

5. You should be inside the virtual machine shortly. Once you are, click on the “Open Folder” button on the left (if you don’t see it, first click on the “Explorer” icon on the left sidebar). A “Open File or Folder” bar should appear to let you type in the directory you want to go to. Type in /var/www/src and click on the “OK” button. 

   ![][image5]

6. Now you should be able to access and edit all the source files. After you’re done coding, simply close your VS Code window. 

   

After you have added your dev machine to VS Code, you can connect to it the next time by following the steps below: 

1. Open your VS Code window and type \> ssh into the command palette at the top (Or press command \+ p to make it appear if you are using a MacBook). Choose “Remote-SSH: Connect to Host” from the drop-down menu.  
   ![][image6]  
2. Select your virtual machine from the drop-down menu and you will be connected in no time. You can proceed to go to the “var/www/src” directory for all the code files by following the steps listed in the previous section.   
   ![][image7]  
   Alternatively, there is a way to go SSH directly into the directory with all the source code files. To do so, follow the steps below:    
1. Type “\> ssh” into the command palette and choose “Remote Explorer” drop-down menu.   
   ![][image8]  
3. You should see your dev machine and the directory you previously opened on the left. Click on the “Connect in New Window” icon (looks like a folder with a plus sign in the upper-left corner) next to the src directory icon and you will be connected to your virtual dev machine with the src directly opened for you.   
   ![][image9]  
     
   Note: After SSH-ing into your dev machine a few times, you should be able to see the src folder of your dev machine appear in the “Recent” section when you open your VS Code window. Simply click on it and you will be connected to your dev machine with the src folder opened for you. No need to go through all the steps listed above anymore.   
     
   Troubleshooting: If you are having trouble connecting to your dev machine, try deleting the .vscode folder and reconnecting. Also, don’t open too many SSH sessions to the same dev machine, which might cause the dev machine to be overloaded and become very slow. For more information, please visit [the official VS Code documentation on SSH sessions](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/remote/ssh).  
     
   Also, if you are getting an error message that says something like “You’re connected to an OS version that is unsupported by Visual Studio Code”, it’s probably because you are using a newer version of VS Code that doesn’t support older Linux distributions. You will need to downgrade to at least VS Code version 1.85 to keep using the dev machine through VS Code. For more information, please visit [this link](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/remote/faq#_can-i-run-vs-code-server-on-older-linux-distributions).   
     
   (Credits to Ali Al Darwish for this section).

##### 	     **How to create a test account on a dev machine when you don’t have access to any of the existing test accounts** {#how-to-create-a-test-account-on-a-dev-machine-when-you-don’t-have-access-to-any-of-the-existing-test-accounts}

1. Log into your dev machine (for detailed instructions, please see [this section](#logging-into-the-developer’s-virtual-machine-⚙️)).   
2. Run cd /var/www/src to get to the source directory where all the code and the Git repository are, and where the make commands work.  
3. Run the following command in the terminal to get the hashed value of your chosen password (replace \<password\> with the password of your choice):

   

   perl \-I /var/www/src/teamassign-lib/lib/ \-MTeamAssignAuthLib \-e 'warn smarter\_crypt(\<password\>)'

4. Copy the generated hashed value to a safe place.   
5. Run “make db” to go into the database.  
6. Run the following command to insert the test account into the database. Replace values in \<\> with what you desire. For \<type\> you can put “admin” or “faculty”. 

   

   insert into person(person\_type,person\_status,first\_name,last\_name,email,school,password) values('admin','active','\<first\_name\>','\<last\_name\>','\<email\>','\<school\>','\<hashed\_value\>');

   

7. Additionally, to add more roles, you can modify the person\_role table. To do so, first find person\_id by doing: 

     
   select person\_id from survey where email=’\<email\>’

   

   Then using the person ID you got from it, run this command to add roles (you do not need to add the role you created an account with originally). 

     
   1= Admin, 2=Faculty, 3=Student, 4= License Manager

     
   Insert into person\_role (person\_id, role\_id) values (\<person\_id\>, \<role\_id\>)

   

8. If you want to update the password of an existing user, run the following SQL command: 

| UPDATE personSET password \= '\<NewHashedPassword\>'WHERE email \= '\<email\>'; |
| :---- |

   

9. Go to “https://\<devNum\>.teamassign.org/login/index” from your browser and log into the account you just created.  
10. (Optional) In the admin interface, give the test account you created an instructor role and student role so you can test both instructor and student features using the same account. To do so:  
1. Click on the “Manage Instructors” button.  
2. Find the account you just created (use the search box if necessary) and click on the name of that account.  
3. On the ‘Instructor Editor’ page, tick the ‘Instructor’ and ‘Student” checkboxes in the lower-left corner next to the title ‘Roles”.   
4. Click the “Save” or “Save or Return” button in the upper-right corner of the page.

	    For more information, please visit [this link](https://github.com/teamassign/Catme-Web/blob/9ee6faf2769708ee15f022da646eaf80e76de72d/docs/cookbook.txt#L4). 

* #### **Useful Web Dev Concepts** {#useful-web-dev-concepts}

  Since TeamAssign is a web application, it is helpful to know some basic computer network terminologies and concepts. They may come in handy when you work on different aspects of TeamAssign. 

  ##### What happens when you type a URL into the browser {#what-happens-when-you-type-a-url-into-the-browser}

  When you type a URL (Ex: teamassign.org/help/login/login2.html) into your browser and hit “enter”, the following things happen (albeit this is a very simplified version):

1. The browser searches for the IP address associated with this domain (teamassign.org) in order to look for the web server that hosts this domain.   
2. The browser will first look into its cache and the caches in its local network, if it can’t find it, it will send queries to other DNS (Domain Name System) servers on the internet.   
3. After the browser finds the web server, it will establish a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection with the server.   
4. The browser will send an HTTP request to the server (in this case, it will be a GET request) to get the text, image, HTML, etc. needed to display the webpage.  
5. The server generates an HTTP response and sends it back to the browser.  
6. The browser renders the content received from the browser and displays the webpage. 

   For more detailed information, please visit [this page](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/what-happens-when-we-type-a-url/) and [this page](https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/what-happens-when-you-type-a-url).  

   

   TeamAssign’s directory corresponds to the URL path. If you need to make changes to any of TeamAssign’s web pages, you can find its location by looking at its URL. In this case, the file login2.html can be found under the directory help/login. 

   ##### HTTP Requests and Responses {#http-requests-and-responses}

* What is an HTTP Request?

  An HTTP request is a message sent from a client to a server requesting a resource such as a web page, image, or file (GET requests), creating a resource (PUT and POST requests), updating a resource (PATCH requests), or deleting a resource from the server (DELETE requests). It usually looks like this: 

  \[HTTP Method\]/\[Request Target URL\]\[HTTP version\]

  \[HTTP Request Header\] 


  For example:

  GET /hello.htm HTTP/1.1

  User-Agent: Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE5.01; Windows NT)

  Host: www.tutorialspoint.com

  Accept-Language: en-us

  Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate

  Connection: Keep-Alive

  For more detailed information, please visit [this page](https://www.tutorialspoint.com/http/http_requests.htm) and [this page](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Messages). 


* Common HTTP Methods  
  * GET: Lets you retrieve data or resource from the server.   
  * POST: Lets you add a resource to the server.   
  * PUT: Lets you replace an existing file or resource. It’s very similar to POST, but the difference is that if you POST the same resource multiple times, duplicates will be created where as if you PUT the same source multiple times, it will simply replace the existing one and you won’t get duplicates.   
  * PATCH: Lets you modify a resource partially.   
  * DELETE: Lets you delete a resource from the server.

    

* What is an HTTP Response

  After you send a HTTP request to the web server, the server will send back an HTTP response to you. It usually looks something like this:


  \[HTTP version\] \[HTTP status code\]

  \[HTTP Header\]

  \[HTTP response body\]


  For example:

  HTTP/1.1 200 OK

  Date: Mon, 27 Jul 2009 12:28:53 GMT

  Server: Apache/2.2.14 (Win32)

  Last-Modified: Wed, 22 Jul 2009 19:15:56 GMT

  Content-Length: 88

  Content-Type: text/html

  Connection: Closed

  \<html\>

  \<body\>

  \<h1\>Hello, World\!\</h1\>

  \</body\>

  \</html\>


  The HTTP status code indicates whether the request was successful, and if not, what kind of error occurred. Some of the most common ones is 200 OK (which means there are no errors) and 404 not found (which means the server couldn’t find the resource you requested). 


  The HTTP response header contains additional information about the client (Ex: time zone, ip address, date, etc.) that are not included in the body. For more information, please visit [this page](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Response_header).


  The HTTP response body contains the information the client requested. In this case, it is a simple HTML file and the client’s browser will use it the render the web page. If the web page is more complicated, the client may send some more HTTP requests to get the CSS and JavaScript files needed to render the web page correctly. 


* #### **About Accessibility** {#about-accessibility}

  ##### What is the Accessibility Project About and Why Is It Important {#what-is-the-accessibility-project-about-and-why-is-it-important}

  The Accessibility Project is an ongoing project at TeamAssign that aims to allow people with disabilities to access TeamAssign just like everyone else (hence the name ‘accessibility’). This is a frontend-focused project that ensures TeamAssign’s user interface is compliant with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), and we update our website when newer versions of these guidelines come out (the latest version is WCAG 2.2). 


  For example, some of these guidelines include making sure there is enough contrast between the color of the text on our website and the background so visually impaired users will not have a hard time reading them. Or make sure there is a text description for every picture shown on the website so users using a screen reader can hear what the picture is about read to them. 

   

  Note that some of our clients will ask for proof that TeamAssign is compliant with the WCAG guidelines before their proposal for TeamAssign usage is approved by their institution. 

##### 	Related Accessibility Documentation {#related-accessibility-documentation}

The most straightforward way to check a website’s accessibility is manual testing. For example, if you are using a MacBook, you can use the VoiceOver tool (it is under System Settings \> Accessibility) to do this. It basically reads the text on websites to users and you can check if the website is accessible to people with disabilities by trying to navigate through the entire website by just using your keyboard.

However, manually checking if our website is compliant with WCAG guidelines can be very tedious, so you can also use browser extensions like Axe DevTools and WAVE Evaluation Tool that check it for you automatically. These tools also show more details like the severity of the issue they detected. For detailed information, please read the [Accessibility Manual for TeamAssign](http://[REDACTED]). 

For other documentation and [TeamAssign’s previous accessibility reports](http://[REDACTED]), please go to TeamAssign’s Google Drive and find the folder named “Accessibility”. 

After you find out which standards TeamAssign is not compliant with, you can go ahead to the codebase, fix the issue, and create a pull request on GitHub for it. After the repo admin reviews it and makes sure there are no further issues, they will merge it to the master branch. 

* #### **About Canvas LMS Integration and Oauth2.0**  {#about-canvas-lms-integration-and-oauth2.0}

  ##### **Overview** {#overview}

  The OAuth 2.0 protocol is being implemented to link TeamAssign and Canvas LMS together (a protocol is a set of procedures for exchanging data between different devices). OAuth 2.0 is the standard protocol these days for allowing a website/application to access user information owned by other web apps without giving out the password directly. If you’ve ever logged into Instagram with Facebook or signed into Twitter with your Google account, then you have already encountered OAuth 2.0. In our case, this happens when an instructor links their TeamAssign account with their Canvas LMS account. After clicking the “Link Canvas” button in the “My Profile” page of your TeamAssign account, the browser redirects to the Canvas LMS SSO login page, where the instructor will enter their credentials for Canvas and give TeamAssign access to their Canvas account. After this, the status of Canvas linking is changed to “Linked” and now the instructor can use various functionalities like importing students, exporting peer evaluation scores, etc. 


  ##### **Terminology** {#terminology}

  Now that you have an idea of what OAuth 2.0 is, we can get into more detail on how it works in TeamAssign. First, let’s define some terms. 


- *Resource owner*: the end-user, people like you and me.  
    
- *Client:* the application trying to access user info. TeamAssign is the client in this case.

- *Authorization server*: the system that authorizes and authenticates the user. Canvas is the authorization server in this case.

- *Authorization grant:* simply put, it’s proof that the user clicked “yes” to the client’s access request. The client takes it to the authorization server to exchange for the access token. 

- *Access token (bearer token):* the key required to gain access to the user information. 

- *Resource server*: the system that holds user information that the client wants to access, it accepts and verifies the access token from the client.

- *Redirect URI*: where the browser redirects to after the user clicks “yes”. 


  Please note that a URI is different from a URL. The main difference is that a URL specifies the location of a resource on the internet, while a URI can used to identify any type of resource, not just those on the internet. Ex: The IBSN of a book. For a more detailed explanation, please visit [this page](https://www.godaddy.com/resources/ae/skills/uri-vs-url).

    
- *Scope*: what the end-user permits the client to do. In this case, TeamAssign is allowed to retrieve a list of courses the instructor teaches, get students enrolled in each course, create group categories, etc. See the “LMS Technical Document” for a comprehensive list of scopes allowed.  
    
- *Client ID, Client Secret*: information used to identify the client to the authorization server when the client is asking the authorization server for an access token/refresh token.   
  


  ##### **Authorization Code Flow 🔄** {#authorization-code-flow-🔄}

  TeamAssign uses the most common OAuth 2.0 flow, authorization code flow, as illustrated below. 


  First, the process starts with the front channel (the browser). 

1. The resource owner (end-user) starts the flow by clicking “Link Canvas”, requesting access to protected resources (the information in the Canvas account to be linked).   
     
   ![Graphical user interface, text, application, emailDescription automatically generated][image11]

2. The client (TeamAssign) sends the redirect URI, response type, and scope requested to the authorization server (Canvas in this case), where the resource owner (end-user) will enter their Canvas credentials for login.   
   ![Graphical user interface, applicationDescription automatically generated][image12]  
     
3. The authorization server asks the resource owner (end-user) for consent to access the resource owner’s Canvas account.   
   ![Graphical user interface, application, TeamsDescription automatically generated][image13]  
     
4. After the resource owner (end-user) clicks “authorize”, the authorization grant is passed back to the client (TeamAssign). The end-user then gets redirected to where the redirect URI leads, which is the “My Profile” page of TeamAssign in this case. Now the status of Canvas linking should be changed to “Linked”.  
   ![Graphical user interface, text, application, emailDescription automatically generated][image14]

	The next steps happen in the backchannel (not being seen by the end-user).

5. The client (TeamAssign) sends an access token request to the authorization server with client\_id and client\_secret to exchange for an access token and a refresh token.  
     
6. The client (TeamAssign) sends the access token to the resource server to access desired user information.   
     
7. Once the resource server verifies the access token, the client (TeamAssign) can have access to the information it needs (the allowed scopes).   
     
   This is all for a high-level explanation of how TeamAssign gets instructor information from Canvas LMS; for more details like how access tokens are stored in the database, please check the “LMS Technical Document”.   
   

   ##### **Source Code 💻** {#source-code-💻}

   This section expands on the “LMS Technical Document” and explains more about how TeamAssign implements the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow. Information present in the “LMS Technical Document” like scopes and databases will only be briefly touched on here; therefore, it is recommended to read the “LMS Technical Document” first and then proceed to this section. 

   

   Related Files:

   TeamAssign-Web/teamassign-lib/lib/LMS/Login.pm,  TeamAssign-Web/teamassign-lib/lib/LMS/Canvas.pm, TeamAssign-Web/teamassign/faculty/my\_profile, TeamAssign-Web/teamassign/faculty/sw40\_students,   TeamAssign-Web/teamassign/faculty/tm\_display\_results, TeamAssign-Web/teamassign/faculty/view\_results. 

   (Most of the files are located under TeamAssign-Web/teamassign-lib/lib/LMS).

   

   Note: the file names will be in *italics* to avoid confusion.

   

1. **Link to Canvas LMS:** If the user clicks “Link Canvas”, *my\_profile* calls get\_auth() in *Login.pm*, which then calls get\_auth() in *Canvas.pm*, which generates $auth\_url with client\_id, redirect\_uri, scopes needed, and uni\_id. $auth\_url is then sent to Canvas, where the end-user will log into their Canvas account and grant TeamAssign access to their account. Next, the end-user gets redirected back to TeamAssign and *my\_profile* saves all the necessary information (person\_id, access\_token, token expiration time, refresh\_token, base\_url, canvas\_user\_id, etc.) into the canvas\_tokens database.   
     
2. **Unlink Canvas:** If the user clicks “Unlink Canvas”, *my\_profile* deletes from the canvas\_tokens database information related to the person\_id of this user. 

3. **Import Students from Canvas for Team Maker surveys:** If an access token is present (meaning we’re already linked to Canvas), *sw40\_students* calls get\_all\_students\_in\_course() from *Canvas.pm*, which sends a request to get all the courses with the access token, and returns the decoded content if the request is successful. Next, for each student, we get the section he or she is in. If any error occurs in this process, we print an error message.

**Import Students from Canvas for Peer Evaluation surveys:** In *sw40\_students*, we first call get\_group\_categories() from *Canvas.pm* and, for each group category, get the group category name. Next, we call get\_groups() from *Canvas.pm*. For each group, we call get\_group\_users() from *Canvas.pm* and set the group user’s team to the group’s team. After that, a CSV file is made with every student included. In *Canvas.pm*, the function get\_all\_students\_in\_course has a while loop to handle pagination. If unspecified, the Canvas LMS API only returns 10 items per page. Since we don’t know how many students there are, we need a while loop to get all the pages and extract all the students. Alternatively, we can add a per\_page parameter to the end of our API call to specify how many items we want Canvas to return per page. This approach is less robust and should only be used when the number of items returned is not too large. For example, the following API call returns 100 users in a Canvas course at a time: 

4. **Import Students from Canvas for Peer Evaluation surveys:** In *sw40\_students*, we first call get\_group\_categories() from *Canvas.pm*, and for each group category, get the group category name. Next, we call get\_groups() from *Canvas.pm*. For each group, we call get\_group\_users() from *Canvas.pm* and set the group user’s team to the group’s team. After that, a CSV file is made with every student included. In *Canvas.pm*, function get\_all\_students\_in\_course has a while loop to handle pagination. If unspecified, the Canvas LMS API only returns 10 items per page. Since we don’t know how many students there are, we need a while loop to get all the pages and extract all the students. Alternatively, we can add a per\_page parameter to the end of our API call to specify how many items we want Canvas to return per page. This approach is less robust and should only be used when the number of items returned is not too big. For example, the following API call returns 100 users in a Canvas course at a time:   
   	http://\<canvas\>/api/v1/courses/:course\_id/users?per\_page=100\&access\_token=\<token\>

5. **Exporting Team Maker groups:** When exporting the made groups to Canvas LMS in *tm\_display\_results*, we first get imported\_class\_id from the database and set it to the course we want to export to. Next, we call get\_course\_list() from *Canvas.pm*, which sends a request to get all the courses with the access token, and returns the decoded content if the request is successful. For every course, add the course ID to the course\_values array, and set the course ID in course\_labels to the course name. When the user clicks “Export to LMS”, we first call get\_group\_categories() from *Canvas.pm*, which gets a list of group categories in the user’s Canvas account using the access token and returns the decoded content. If a group category already exists with the same activity name, we delete it. Next, we call create\_group\_category() from *Canvas.pm*, which creates a new group category with the given name and returns the ID of the new group. Within this group category, we create a group for each team formed by Team Maker by calling create\_group() from *Canvas.pm* and adding all the team members to this group. We print a success message if there are no errors and an error message otherwise.

6. **Exporting Peer Evaluation grades:** Same as exporting Team maker groups, we first set the course we want to export to equal to the course we imported from, call get\_course\_list() from *Canvas.pm*, add the course id to course\_values array, and set course id in course\_labels to the course name. Next, we check if an assignment already exists for the selected course ID, if it does, we delete it and create a new one. For each student, we get their grade depending on whether the instructor included the adjustment factor or not, and call grade\_student\_assignment() from *Canvas.pm*, which posts the grade to Canvas. We print a success message if there are no errors and an error message otherwise. 

7. **Request Access Token with Refresh Token When the Previous Access Token Expires:** This is done in *Canvas.pm* using check\_and\_update\_token(). It first gets the expire\_at (expire time), base\_url, refresh\_token, client\_id, and client\_secret from the database. Next, if we are one minute past the expiration time, send a request for another access token with the client\_id, client\_secret, grant\_type, and refresh\_token. If the request is successful, decode the new access token and update the access\_token and expire\_at in the database. check\_and\_update\_token() gets called in almost every function in *Canvas.pm* when we need to access information or modify something in the user’s Canvas account.

* #### **Navigating AWS (Amazon Web Services)**  {#navigating-aws-(amazon-web-services)}

  ##### **What is AWS ☁️** {#what-is-aws-☁️}

  AWS stands for [Amazon Web Services](https://aws.amazon.com/). It is one of the most popular cloud computing platforms nowadays that utilizes the pay-as-you-go model. What this means is that businesses and organizations can “rent” computing machines from AWS to host servers, deploy applications, etc. This allows organizations to focus on their products because they won’t have to take care of the infrastructure. You can specify what kind of machine, how much storage, etc., you want and be charged different prices depending on your choice. If your need for computing resources increases, you can just switch to another instance with better computing power anytime, so there is no need to plan ahead for provisioning. On the contrary, if you no longer need an instance, you can always stop it and delete it, so you won’t be charged. Other popular cloud computing providers include Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud Platform (GCP), but in the case of TeamAssign, we’re using AWS. 


  ##### **AWS Account Access** {#aws-account-access}

  URL: [https://aws.amazon.com/](https://aws.amazon.com/)

  Account: \[REDACTED\]

  Password: \[REDACTED\]


  ##### **Launching an AWS instance to host Canvas LMS** {#launching-an-aws-instance-to-host-canvas-lms}

  For convenience, you can just create a new instance using the settings from a pre-existing AWS instance. To do this, follow the instructions below:


1. Go to [https://aws.amazon.com/](https://aws.amazon.com/) and sign in using the account and password listed in the previous section.  
2. Navigate to Services (on the top left corner with an icon that looks like nine squares) \> Compute (under All services) \> EC2. Alternatively, type EC2 in the search bar and click on it.   
     
   ![Graphical user interface, text, applicationDescription automatically generated][image15]  
     
3. Now you should be able to see a dashboard with all the instances. To launch an AWS instance identical to a pre-existing one, right-click on the Instance ID of the instance you want to create \> Images and templates \> Launch more like this.   
     
   ![Graphical user interface, text, applicationDescription automatically generated][image16]  
     
4. Since you are using the same deployment settings as a pre-existing AWS instance, you should be automatically taken to Step 7: Review Instance Launch. When you click on “Launch”, you will be prompted to provide a key pair used to SSH into this particular AWS instance. You can either choose an existing key pair or create a new key pair. Create a new key pair if you don’t have access to any of the existing key pair files. If you need to create a new key pair, you can either do it here or create a new key pair separately and then choose it in this window.

   ![Graphical user interface, text, application, emailDescription automatically generated][image17]

   

5. After this click “Launch Instance”.   
     
6. SSH into your newly launched AWS instance. Detailed instructions can be found in [this link](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/AccessingInstancesLinux.html).   
   

##### **Creating a new key pair 🔐** {#creating-a-new-key-pair-🔐}

1. Sign in to AWS and navigate to Network & Security \> Key Pairs.   
     
   ![Graphical user interface, text, application, emailDescription automatically generated][image18]  
     
2. Click “Create key pair” on the top right corner.   
     
   ![Graphical user interface, text, application, emailDescription automatically generated][image19]  
     
3. Enter the name for your key pair and choose the key pair type, private key file format, and add tags if you want to. Note: you can only use ED25519 keys with Linux and Mac instances.    
     
   ![Graphical user interface, applicationDescription automatically generated][image20]  
     
4. Click “Create key pair”. Now you should be able to see your new key pair on the Key Pairs dashboard. 

   ##### **Allocating an elastic address and connecting to an AWS instance** {#allocating-an-elastic-address-and-connecting-to-an-aws-instance}

   When you try to SSH into your AWS instance, you need either the instance’s public DNS name (Public IPv4 DNS name) or Public IPv4 address, but they might not appear on your EC2 instance dashboard. If this happens, try the two following fixes:

   

1. Enable DNS hostnames to show.  
1. Type “VPC” in the search bar \> click “Your VPCs” on the left sidebar under “Virtual Private Cloud” \> select your VPC \> click “Actions” on the top right corner \> select “Edit DNS hostnames \> click “Enable” under DNS hostnames \> click “Save Changes”

2. If enabling DNS hostnames to show doesn’t fix the problem, create a new Elastic IP address and associate it with your instance.  
1. Type “Elastic IP addresses” in the search bar or choose “Elastic IPs” under “Network & Security” \> click “Allocate Elastic IP address” on the top right corner \> click “Allocate” 

   

   ![Graphical user interface, text, application, chat or text messageDescription automatically generated][image21]

2. At the Elastic IP address dashboard, click on the Allocate IPv4 address you just created \> click “Associate Elastic IP address” on the top right corner \> choose your instance \> click “Associate”

   

   ![Graphical user interface, applicationDescription automatically generated][image22]

   

   	![Graphical user interface, applicationDescription automatically generated][image23]

   ##### **SSH into your AWS instance** {#ssh-into-your-aws-instance}

   After launching your AWS instance, you need to be able to access it via SSH. If you created a new key pair file in the previous steps (the .pem file you need to SSH into your AWS instance), you need to download it onto your local machine. After the download is complete, navigate to the directory that contains your key pair file and run the following command: 

   

		chmod 600 key-pair-file-name.pem

This command means changing the file permissions so only the owner of the .pem file has full read and write access to it. You need to do this for security reasons or else you won’t be allowed to SSH into your AWS instance. 

Now you should be able to get the Public IPv4 DNS name/Public IPv4 address from the EC2 instance dashboard and use them to SSH into your instance. 

![Graphical user interface, applicationDescription automatically generated][image24]

Use the following commands to SSH into your AWS instance (both work, you can use either):   
ssh \-i \<key-pair filename\> ec2-user@public-ipv4-address   or  
ssh \-i \<key-pair filename\> ec2-user@public-ipv4-dns

##### **How to SSH into an AWS instance if you don’t have its key-pair file** {#how-to-ssh-into-an-aws-instance-if-you-don’t-have-its-key-pair-file}

In this case, you will need to [add a key-pair file of yours to the AWS EC2 instance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/replacing-key-pair.html) and SSH into it using that key-pair file. 

* #### **Setting up Canvas** {#setting-up-canvas}

  To test the Canvas-related functionalities of TeamAssign, we use a Canvas instance hosted on AWS. Our current Canvas instance is a simpler version hosted in Docker containers that lacks several features but is still enough for testing purposes. If you need to set everything up from scratch, go to the official Canvas LMS GitHub repository, git clone the source code, install all the needed dependencies (git, homebrew, docker, docker-compose, mutagen, mutagen-compose, dory, etc.), and run the setup script. You might also need to do some additional environment configurations depending on which AWS instance you are using or what version of dependencies you installed. For more information, see [here](https://github.com/instructure/canvas-lms/wiki/Quick-Start). 


  Note: At the time you are reading this, Canvas may have been updated, so the dependencies you need to install may not be the same as the ones listed above. Also, the commands to install different dependencies may be different from what is listed in the installation guide. For example, the guide tells you to install git using “apt-get”, but Amazon Linux actually uses “yum” as its package manager for installing software. You will have to do some Googling to figure out the right commands for the installation. 


1. SSH into the Canvas instance. You can find the public IPv4 address of this instance from the EC2 dashboard under the name “Canvas-new-3”.  
     
2. Run “cd canvas-lms” to go into the “canvas-lms” directory. If the Canvas instance is not running already, start it up by running the following command:   
   

   ./script/docker\_dev\_setup.sh  
     
   (This command will take quite a while to run. It will prompt you to create a Canvas account. For testing purposes, the email address you should use is \[REDACTED\])  
     
3. Run mutagen-compose up \-d to start up all the containers. To check the status of Docker containers, run docker ps \-a   
     
4. Copy the URL “[http://localhost/](http://localhost/)” into your browser, where localhost should be replaced with the public IPv4 address/public IPv4 DNS of this AWS instance (same as the one you used to SSH into this instance).  
     
5. You should see the login page. Enter the credentials from step 3, and there you go\! You are successfully logged into Canvas.   
     
6. On the left sidebar, click Admin \> Site Admin \> Developer Keys \> \+ Developer Key \> \+ API Key  
     
   ![Graphical user interface, text, application, emailDescription automatically generated][image25]  
     
   ![Graphical user interface, applicationDescription automatically generated][image26]  
     
7. Enter the Key Name, Owner Email (\[REDACTED\]), Redirect URIs (https://dev01.teamassign.org/faculty/my\_profile), toggle Enforce Scopes on the right side, and select the scopes needed (the scopes can be found in the “LMS Technical Document”). Click “Save Key”. Note: Sometimes you have to put the redirect URI in both “Redirect URIs” and “Redirect URI (Legacy)” to make things work properly.   
     
   ![Graphical user interface, text, applicationDescription automatically generated][image27]  
     
8. A new developer key is created. The client\_id is the string of digits under “Details” and the client\_secret is the string of alphabets that appears when you click “Show Key” under “Details”.  
   ![A picture containing diagramDescription automatically generated][image28]  
     
9. Now it’s time to connect TeamAssign to Canvas. Go to “https://dev01.teamassign.org/login/index”, and log in using the faculty account (email: \[REDACTED\], password: \[REDACTED\]).   
     
10. In the upper right corner, change the role to “Administrator”. Scroll to the bottom and click “Add Institution LMS Info”.  
      
11. Enter the institution, LMS Base URL (http://public-ipv4-dns:8900/), LMS Client ID (see step 8), LMS Client Secret (see step 8), Email domain (school.edu), and LMS type (Canvas). Click “Save”.   
      
12. Click “Cancel” to return to the Administrative Interface. In the upper right corner, change the role to “instructor”. Go to “My Profile” \> Link Canvas. If everything goes right, you should be able to log into Canvas and get redirected back to TeamAssign’s My Profile page with the “Link Canvas” button changed to “Unlink Canvas”. A visual demo can be found in the *Authorization Code Flow* section under About Canvas LMS Integration and OAuth 2.0 of this document.  
      
13.  If for some reason you need to set up a Canvas instance from scratch, clone the Canvas GitHub repository and go to the “Installation” section in [this link](https://github.com/instructure/canvas-lms). 

    

    Note: Canvas requires a lot of memory to run, so be sure to pick a larger instance type to host Canvas to avoid under-provisioning. Also, some commands in the installation guide might not work depending on what type of AWS instance you are using. For example, Amazon Linux uses “yum” rather than “apt-get” when installing packages. You will need to Google a bit to find the right way to install all the needed dependencies.   ##### **How to SIS import (batch upload) using a CSV file in Canvas** {#how-to-sis-import-(batch-upload)-using-a-csv-file-in-canvas}

  	Under the folder “CSV Files for Testing” in this Google Drive, there are several files that are formatted in a way Canvas accepts and can be used to test if there are any issues when importing from Canvas to TeamAssign. There is a file called “courses.csv” that can be used to create fake Canvas courses and two files named “sysiphus\_users.csv” and “sysiphus\_enrollment.csv”, which are used to create fake students. To import files, log in to your Canvas account, then go to Admin \> TeamAssign (or any username you set previously) \> SIS Import (on the left side) \> Choose File \> Upload your CSV file from your computer \> Process Data.  
    
  	![][image29]  
    
    
  	![][image30]  
    
   	When testing, first import “courses.csv” so we have courses to import students to. Next, add yourself as a “Teacher” to the desired course (you must ***not*** skip this step or the course won’t show up on your dashboard and the API calls won’t return it, causing the course to not appear on the TeamAssign side; see detailed instructions on how to do so in the next section below). Then, import “sysiphus\_users.csv” to get these users onto the Canvas system. Finally, import “sysiphus\_enrollment.csv” to enroll the students in the desired courses. Note: **DO NOT** create students manually in the Canvas system; always add them in the CSV file and then add them to the desired course via SIS import. If you create students manually in the Canvas system, enrollments will have to be confirmed by those students via email for them to officially be in the course; otherwise, their emails and the Canvas API will not return some other necessary information. This will cause problems on the TeamAssign side when generating a CSV file, and the import will fail.   
  	

For more information on how the CSV files are structured, see [this link](https://community.canvaslms.com/t5/Admin-Guide/How-do-I-format-CSV-text-files-for-uploading-SIS-data-into-a/ta-p/216) and [this link](https://canvas.instructure.com/doc/api/file.sis_csv.html). 

	For more information on Canvas SIS Import, see [here](https://community.canvaslms.com/t5/Admin-Guide/How-do-I-import-SIS-data-to-a-Canvas-account/ta-p/98). 

##### **How to manually add people to a Canvas course** {#how-to-manually-add-people-to-a-canvas-course}

1.  After logging into your Canvas account, click on the course you want to add people to.   
2. Click on “People” on the left sidebar.   
3. Click on the “+ People” button in the upper-right corner. An “Add People” pop-up screen should appear.   
4. Choose whether you want to add users by email address, login ID, or SIS ID. Enter the email address/login ID/SIS ID in the text box below. When adding multiple users, use a comma or line break to separate users.  
5. Choose the role and section of your users (student, teacher, TA, designer, or observer) and click “Next” in the lower-right corner.   
6. Click “Add Users,” and you’re done\!

  ##### **TeamAssign’s Mentoring Feature**  {#teamassign’s-mentoring-feature}

  The Mentoring feature allows instructors to participate in surveys to rate and guide students, but they themselves will not be evaluated like a regular team member. Since this feature requires allowing a person (the mentor) to be on more than one team, which contradicts one of the primary premises TeamAssign is built upon, many major changes have been made to our codebase to make it work. Currently, it is still in the beta-testing phase, so there may be frequent bug reports about it (the bug reports may not be obvious that their issue is caused by the mentoring feature). For more details about the mentoring feature, please visit [this link](http://[REDACTED]). 

* #### **Working with [GitHub](https://github.com/teamassign/Catme-Web)** {#working-with-github}

  ##### Creating a Pull Request {#creating-a-pull-request}

  A pull request is also called a merge request. It happens when developers complete a feature, bug fix, etc., and want to incorporate their code into the main branch (the official version of the code) of the GitHub repository.    
    
  Steps:   
1. You don’t have to fork and clone the TeamAssign GitHub repository; you should already have a copy on your dev machine. Create a new branch using the command: 

   git checkout \-b \<new\_branch\>

   

   Note that usually, you would want to create a branch from the master branch so your code doesn’t get mixed up with the changes from other branches. To do so, run git checkout master to switch to the master branch. Now, if you run git checkout \-b \<new\_branch\>, the new branch will be created from the master branch. P.S. The master branch is the equivalent of the main branch in more recent Git repositories. GitHub renamed “master” to “main” a while ago; since TeamAssign’s codebase is fairly old, the place where our code is located is still called ‘master’. 

   

2. Run git branch to verify you are on the new branch just created. This command will show you all the branches stemming from the repository. The branch you are on will have a “\*” on the left of its name. 

   

3. You should already have an upstream repository usually named “origin”. To see what the name of your upstream repository is, run the command git remote \-v. This will show you all the upstream repositories. Next, go ahead and make changes to the code. 

   

4. After you finish coding/debugging, run git status to see which files you modified. 

   

5. Run git add \<file\> for files you want to commit. If there are a lot of files to add, just run git add \-A to stage all (including new, modified, and deleted) files. 

   

6. Run git commit \-m “some commit message” to commit the files you added. 

   

7. Push your code to your branch by running: 

   git push \<upstream\_repository\> \<new\_branch\>

   (The upstream repository is usually named “origin”). 

   

8. If the previous step is successful, you should get a message in your terminal window telling you where to go the create a pull request. Visit that URL, write down your title and comments, and click “Create pull request”. 

   

9. Now you just have to wait for others to review your code. They might ask you to make additional changes before merging your branch with the main branch. But other than that, you’re all done\!

   

   

   For more information on how to push code from your local machine to GitHub, please see [this link](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/importing-your-projects-to-github/importing-source-code-to-github/adding-locally-hosted-code-to-github). 

   

##### Linking a Pull Request to an Issue {#linking-a-pull-request-to-an-issue}

Very often, you will run into this scenario: You were assigned a GitHub issue to work on, and you have successfully figured out the solution and coded it up. Now you need to create a pull request on GitHub for this fix. This is when you will need to link your pull request to the issue you have fixed. It is actually really simple, just put Fixes \#\<the ID of GitHub issue you have fixed\> when you are prompted to write a pull request comment on *the GitHub website* (Note: not the commit message when you run the git commit \-m “\<some commit message\>” command on your dev machine). For more information on this and other ways to link pull requests to GitHub issues, please visit [GitHub’s official documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/linking-a-pull-request-to-an-issue). 

##### Duplicating a Commit to another Branch {#duplicating-a-commit-to-another-branch}

Sometimes you will want to duplicate the changes of a specific commit on a branch to another branch. You can accomplish this by using the git cherry-pick command. To do so, follow the steps below: 

1. First, switch to the branch that has the commit you want to copy by doing git checkout \<branch name\>.   
2. Next, run git log to see the commit history. You should see a bunch of information from previous commits, such as commit ID, author, commit message, and commit date.   
3. Copy the commit ID of the commit you need.   
4. Switch to the branch you want to copy the commit to by running git checkout \<branch name\>.   
5. Run git cherry-pick \<commit ID\> and the commit with that commit ID you have just used in the git cherry-pick command will be copied to this branch. 

Please note that the git cherry-pick command should only be used **when absolutely necessary**. For more information, please visit [this tutorial](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/cherry-pick). 

##### Other Tips {#other-tips}

1. It is best to treat your local main/master branch as read-only, that is, always create a separate branch off of main/master and do your work from there. Don’t modify the local main/master branch directly.   
2. It’s a good idea to always keep your local main/master branch up to date. To do so, run git pull origin master before starting your work. This will get you the most recent git checkout (which is the newest version of the code). You should also run make update after that to restart the server. You may also need to run make update\_db (if there are changes to the database and you need to run a SQL migration) or make update\_cpanlib (if there are new dependencies to be installed) if necessary. This ensures everything works properly.   
3. Be very careful when you create a new branch. If you want to create a branch off of main/master, you need to be on main/master when you run git checkout \-b \<new\_branch\>. If you are on some random branch, then the new branch will be created off of that random branch, which will contain all the changes the random branch has. Doing work off of such a branch could potentially cause issues since the modifications you made and the changes on the original random branch are all mixed together.   
4. If you need to discard all changes in a file, run git checkout \-- \<path\_to\_file\>.   
5. If you want to undo a git add command, run git reset \<path\_to\_file\>. If you want to remove every file you just git added, simply run git reset.   
6.  If you want to view a previous commit, first run git log to view the commit history (it will show you the ID, author, date, and name of all previous commits. Copy the commit ID of the commit you want to view and then run git checkout \<commit\_id\>.   
        

* #### **TeamAssign Database 📊**  {#teamassign-database-📊}

  TeamAssign uses PostgreSQL as its database. The syntax of PostgreSQL is very similar to that of MySQL, but there are still some differences. In this section, we will explain the basics of the TeamAssign database. 


  ##### How to Enter the TeamAssign Database {#how-to-enter-the-teamassign-database}

1. First, log into your dev machine via SSH and run “cd /var/www/src” to go to the location of the source code. For more details, please see the [Logging into the developer’s virtual machine](#logging-into-the-developer’s-virtual-machine-⚙️) section above.   
2. Run “make db” to enter the PostgreSQL database interface. 

   ##### Commands {#commands}

   List all tables in the current schema:   
   \\dt   
     
   Press the space bar afterward to make all rows appear and press q to stop listing tables (the same rule applies to listing table records).  
     
   List the contents of a specific table:  
    table \<table\_name\>;  
     
   List the schema of a specific table:  
   	 \\d \<table\_name\>;  
     
   Counting records example:  
   	select count(id) from \<table\_name\> where \<insert critieria\>;  
     
   Listing records with specific criteria examples (similar to MySQL syntax):   
1. select \* from \<table\_name\> where \<column\> \= \<string\_to\_match\>;  
   (this returns all rows whose \<column\> content matches \<string\_to\_match\>)  
     
2. select \* from \<table\_name\> where \<column\> like ‘%” || \<substring\_to\_match\> || ‘%’;  
   (this returns all rows whose \<column\> content contains the substring \<substring\_to\_match\>)  
     
   Update contents of a specific table:  
   	Update \<table\_name\> set \<column\> \= \<updated\_data\> where \<criteria\>

   Exit database:

   	\\q

That is all. Congratulations on making it to the end\! 🎉🎉🎉
